theme: Holiness for priests and people; sacred things
readingInstruction: Read Leviticus 20:1-22:33. These chapters continue the Holiness Code with penalties for serious sin, and with strict rules for the priests. Watch for the repeated reasons God gives for his commands.
settingTheScene: Chapter 20 lists punishments for the offenses named in chapters 18 and 19, including child sacrifice, occult practices, and various sexual sins. Chapters 21 and 22 return to the priests and the sacred offerings, setting a higher standard for those who serve at the altar. The reading is demanding, and some of it is hard to take in. It is important to remember that these were laws for Israel as a nation under the old covenant, in a time and a place very different from ours.
observation: The laws of chapter 20 are tied to the command, “Consecrate yourselves, and be holy, for I am the LORD your God” (20:7-8).
God says, “You shall be holy to me, for I the LORD am holy and have separated you from the peoples, that you should be mine” (20:26).
The punishments are severe, including death for some offenses, because the land itself will “vomit you out” if it is defiled (20:22).
The priests must avoid contact with the dead, except for close family, and are to be careful about marriage (21:1-15).
A priest with a physical defect may eat the holy food, but may not approach the altar (21:16-23).
Unclean priests may not eat the holy things until they are cleansed (22:1-9).
“You shall not profane my holy name, that I may be sanctified among the people of Israel. I am the LORD who sanctifies you” (22:32).
interpretation:
The refrain of this section is the double statement of God’s character and God’s work: “I am the LORD who sanctifies you.” In chapter 20, the people are told to consecrate themselves and be holy. In 20:8 God says he is the one who makes them holy. In 21:8 and 22:32 he says it again. The call to holiness is not a demand to make yourself holy by effort. It is a call to live in line with what God has already done by choosing and setting apart his people.

The severity of the penalties is meant to be understood in context. In a nation where God lived among the people in the tabernacle, serious sin was not just a private matter. It threatened the whole community, because it defiled the land and the sanctuary. The penalties show how serious these sins were in God’s eyes. They also show that Israel, as a theocracy, had a unique role. We should not read these laws as a model for modern governments. The New Testament shows that the church does not carry the sword, and that discipline in the church takes the form of rebuke and exclusion (1 Corinthians 5).

The restrictions on the priests are another picture of the holiness of God. A priest must be physically whole and ritually clean. He serves a God of perfect holiness, and the priest’s own body is meant to reflect it. These regulations may seem harsh, especially the rule about physical defects. But they were not a judgment of a person’s worth. A priest with a defect still ate the holy food and shared in the priestly benefits. The point was to picture the perfection of the one who would come to be the true priest.

And note again that offerings had to be without blemish. God deserves the best. It is a theme that runs from Cain and Abel to Malachi, where God rebukes the people for bringing blind and lame animals (Malachi 1:8). What we give to God shows what we think of him.
connection: Jesus is the priest without defect, “holy, innocent, unstained, separated from sinners” (Hebrews 7:26), and the lamb “without blemish or spot” (1 Peter 1:19). Paul says that Christ “gave himself up for her, that he might sanctify her” (Ephesians 5:25-26), and that “God has called us not for impurity, but in holiness” (1 Thessalonians 4:7). Peter calls believers “a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation” (1 Peter 2:9).
application:
Reflect on the statement, “I am the LORD who sanctifies you.” Thank God that your holiness depends on his work.

Ask whether you are giving God your best, or what is left over.

Pray for the leaders of your church, that they would be examples of holiness.
prayerPrompts: Thank God for setting you apart as his own.
Ask him to help you give him your best.
Thank him for Jesus, the perfect priest and spotless lamb.
